name: Nathaniel Moran
stance: Co-sponsor of a bipartisan requirement that frontier AI developers keep a government-ordered shutdown capability.

statements.text: The next frontier isn’t just AI itself—it’s AI doing its own research and development.
We must urgently assess how far Chinese AI systems have come—and work with U.S. industry to contain the risks of automated AI R&D.

This shift may be the most significant technological development since the internet. But unlike past tech waves, the systems we’re creating now are beginning to learn faster than we can regulate, adapt, or even fully understand.
statements.outlet: Office of Rep. Moran (op-ed in The Hill)

statements.text: If the U.S. fails to lead in the responsible development of automated AI systems, we risk more than economic decline. We risk ceding control of a future shaped by black-box algorithms and self-directed machines, some of which do not align with democratic values or basic human safety.
statements.outlet: Office of Rep. Moran (op-ed in The Hill)

statements.text: But I firmly believe that the pace and depth of this discussion (and resulting action) must quicken and intensify, before the next generation of AI systems begins writing the future without us in the loop.
statements.outlet: Office of Rep. Moran (op-ed in The Hill)

statements.text: This is not a call for sweeping regulation, nor is it a call for alarm. It’s a call to avoid falling asleep at the controls.
statements.outlet: Office of Rep. Moran (op-ed in The Hill)

statements.text: When it comes to national security and public safety implications, information from the private sector about what these models are doing and what they're capable of is imperative to protecting Americans.

The private AI companies on the frontline of developing these systems are the canaries in the mine. When they see a national security or public safety threat, we need to know. That's the AI Incident Reporting Act.
With transparency about AI systems, the private sector can largely regulate itself, and we can protect national security and public safety.
This is exactly the scenario my AI Incident Reporting Act addresses, requiring developers report dangerous AI behavior to @CommerceGov.
Co-introduced the AI Kill Switch Act (H.R. 9917) with Rep. Lieu.
Stewardship means making sure humans keep the capability to control the technology we build.
My AI Incident Reporting Act is a straightforward answer: keep innovating, but if an AI model evades its safeguards or threatens critical infrastructure, you can't stay silent.
Our bill, the AI Kill Switch Act, with Rep. Ted Lieu requires the largest AI developers to maintain real shutdown controls, with DHS able to act in a true emergency.
The folks building frontier AI models are telling us themselves: they need a kill switch.
More and more AI models are beginning to escape their intended boundaries, and fall outside human control.
That's why @RepTedLieu and I introduced the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Act: the most powerful AI systems must always have a human who can shut them off.
But, Congress cannot ignore the realities of AI and the potential risks that come with it. Innovation and safety are not mutually exclusive.
We have a real opportunity to get AI right, but only if both parties, frontier developers, and safety leaders come to the table together.
Capitol Hill will never move at the speed of AI innovation, and it shouldn't try to legislate from behind.

Just like when you go back to the Cold War, when the United States was engaging with the Soviet Union on ICBMs and nuclear weapons, we wanted to make sure that we were talking with our adversary on a technology that could be very dangerous and making sure that we are in agreement on how to preserve safety for all of humanity. We certainly should be doing that with China.
The U.S. is ahead, and Washington shouldn't rush to overregulate.
Said in a Breitbart interview that the U.S. has leverage for an AI deal with China because China depends on U.S. chips.
We're 3-6 months ahead of China in AI development. That lead didn't happen by accident, and we can't regulate it away.
Our AI Kill Switch Act, with @tedlieu, also builds in accountability, requiring companies to report incidents to DHS.
Congress cannot rush to legislate on such a high-stakes issue like AI. Prudence—not politics—should drive our policymaking.
Discussed on a podcast how America can lead on AI without losing control of it, including the case for a kill switch and mandatory reporting when models slip human control.
As more AI incidents come to light, the US Gov & companies need dependable reporting mechanisms to verify what is happening.
In order for you to drive your vehicle as fast as you can down the interstate of innovation, you have to have a brake in it.
I'm encouraged by the dialogue and the Joint Commitment from President Trump's historic meeting with Tech leaders today.
